The LLM system writes tests designed to fail on risky diffs, and caught 74 privacy SEVs before landing in H1 2026, with a 60% engineer-reported true-positive rate. The post Meet Meta’s JiTTests: LLM-Generated Tests Designed to Fail Before Risky Code Lands appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Meta has moved Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests) from research prototype into its production infrastructure . Meta JiTTests is an LLM-based system that writes executable tests designed to fail on a risky code change. A failing test is concrete evidence that a diff changed behavior. Meta team reports that JiTTests caught 74 privacy SEVs at the diff stage in the first half of 2026. The method is described in the FSE 2026 research paper ‘Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta ‘. TL;DR Scale: Runs on Meta backend code with hundreds of millions of lines. The research paper analyzes 22,126 generated tests. Runs on: Meta’s internal infrastructure, overnight on spare capacity. Judge models in the paper: Llama3.3-70B, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4. Not publicly available. Performance: Engineers report a 60% true-positive rate at full scale (self-reported). Best: 74 privacy SEVs caught before landing in H1 2026; privacy SEV occurrence down 20%. Worst: The initial deployment confirmed only 8 of 41 reported catches (19.5%). Bottom line: Best: executable proof of a bug before merge. Worst: internal only, with self-reported numbers. What are Catching JiTTests? Catching JiTTests are LLM-generated tests that should fail when a diff introduces a bug. Traditional hardening tests pass when written and guard against future regressions. Catching tests target the change under review, before it lands. Meta formalized the details in its 2025 paper ‘Harden and Catch’ . Most AI bug tools act like faster human reviewers. They read the diff and leave comments. JiTTests instead execute code and show a concrete behavioral difference. Meta team concedes this takes more computational steps. It argues the approach catches bug classes that LLM or agent review can miss. How does the JiTTests pipeline work? The production pipeline has 5 stages: Targeting: Runs overnight on spare capacity. It selects the previous day’s risky diffs, using a mechanism similar to Meta’s Diff Risk Score. Test generation: 2 diff-aware workflows produce candidate tests (explained below). LLM-as-Judge ensemble: Several LLMs score each failing test using the test code, failure trace, diff and inferred intent. RubFake: The Rule-Based False-Positive Killing Environment adds deterministic checks. Its rules flag patterns like reflection, broken mocks and not-implemented exceptions. Human-on-the-loop: The system decides whether to contact an engineer, based on the combined ranking. Dodgy diff vs intent-aware: what is the difference? The dodgy diff workflow assumes every diff is buggy. It treats the diff as a mutant of its parent and generates tests that tell them apart. The intent-aware workflow first infers what the diff should do from its code, title and summary. It lists risks, builds a mutant for each, and writes tests to kill them. Tests that then fail on the real diff become ‘weak catches.’ What do the benchmarks show? The research team analyzes 22,126 generated tests. Diff-aware methods produced 4x more candidate catches than hardening tests. They produced 20x more than tests that failed by coincidence. The intent-aware workflow produced weak catches in 6.4% of its tests and on 7.9% of diffs. Dodgy diff scored 2.5% and 4.0%. Meta’s earlier ACH mutation-guided hardening scored 0.8% and 1.6%. The rule-based and LLM assessors cut human review load by 70%. Feature Catching JiTTests, intent-aware Catching JiTTests, dodgy diff ACH mutation-guided TestGen-LLM Org / first published Meta, 2026 Meta, 2026 Meta, 2025 Meta, FSE 2024 Goal Catch bugs in the diff under review Catch bugs in the diff under review Harden code against specific fault classes Improve existing human-written tests Generated test should Fail on a buggy diff Fail on a buggy diff Pass when generated Pass when generated Aware of the diff Yes, infers intent and risks Yes, intent-unaware No No Weak catches per test* 6.4% (52 of 811) 2.5% (41 of 1,621) 0.8% (6 of 754) 2.0% (89 of 4,499) Diffs with a weak catch* 7.9% 4.0% 1.6% 3.6% False-positive filter LLM judge ensemble + RubFake rules LLM judge ensemble + RubFake rules Not disclosed Build, pass and coverage filters Public availability Internal only Internal only Internal only Internal only *Figures from Table 1 of the JiTTests paper (self-reported, Meta codebase). TestGen-LLM row uses the “need not add coverage” setting. A weak catch is a candidate failure, not a confirmed bug. What changed at full scale? The initial deployment was modest. Meta reported 41 candidate catches to engineers. 8 were confirmed true positives, a 19.5% rate. 4 of those would have caused serious failures in production. The October 2026 engineering post reports much stronger production numbers: 589 engineers engaged with JiTTests, 64% of those contacted. Engineers reported a 60% true-positive rate. 74 privacy SEVs were caught at the diff stage in the first half of 2026. Overall privacy SEV occurrence fell 20% in the same period. What does human-on-the-loop mean? Human-in-the-loop means a person reviews every output. Human-on-the-loop means engineers set criteria and monitor results in aggregate. They intervene at the policy level, not on each test. Meta team rarely need to read test code. They only confirm whether an observed behavior change was intended. Can developers use JiTTests? The answer is No. JiTTests is internal Meta infrastructure. Meta has not released code, models or an API. Teams can still copy the pattern: diff-aware mutation-guided test generation, an LLM judge ensemble, deterministic filters and aggregate human oversight. Key Takeaways Meta’s JiTTests writes LLM tests meant to fail on buggy diffs. 74 privacy SEVs caught pre-merge in H1 2026; privacy SEVs down 20%. Engineers report a 60% true-positive rate, up from 19.5% in the paper. Intent-aware tests hit weak catches at 6.4%, vs 0.8% for ACH hardening. Internal only: no code, model or API released. The post Perplexity Computer Adds Multiagent: Up to 16 AI Agents That Cross-Check Work appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Perplexity has added Multiagent to Computer , its agent platform for research and multistep work. Perplexity Computer Multiagent is a new effort level that sits above Ultra. A lead agent runs a team of agents on different frontier models. Those agents work in parallel, share findings directly and check each other’s work. For developers and analysts, the change is structural. Supporting agents no longer report only to a single lead. TL;DR Size: Up to 16 agents per task, plus the lead. Context length: Not disclosed. Runs on: Perplexity’s cloud. Web only, Perplexity Max plan. No local or quantized option. Performance: Not benchmarked. Perplexity published no accuracy or speed numbers. Best: 16-agent cap with direct agent-to-agent checks across 3 default model families (Claude, GPT, Gemini). What is Perplexity Computer Multiagent? Multiagent is the highest effort level in Perplexity Computer. It coordinates AI models to analyze complex tasks and cross-check their work, per Perplexity’s announcement . It builds on effort controls launched on September 17, 2026 . That release added 4 settings: Light, Standard, High and Ultra. Each setting picks the orchestrator model and its reasoning depth. Lower settings use less expensive models. How does Multiagent work? The lead agent plans the task and assigns parts to supporting agents. It can assign up to 16 agents and also does part of the work itself. In Perplexity’s example, Claude Fable 5.2 plans the task. It splits work among agents running Claude Opus 5.5, GPT 6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Carbon. Those 3 models form the default team. Fable 5.2 and GPT 6 Astra join as supporting agents only when requested or needed. Key mechanics from the launch post : Direct sharing: Agents use evidence found by others, question assumptions and flag discrepancies. Shared files: Agents coordinate edits to shared files. One agent can update revenue assumptions and notify another to reuse them in a valuation. Single point of contact: Users talk only to the lead. The lead merges findings into one response. Follow-ups: The lead tells affected agents what changed. The team continues its existing work. Control: Users see which agents and models are running. Stopping the thread stops the whole team. Model choice: Users can name specific models in their query. Multiagent vs Ultra vs Model Council Perplexity now offers 3 ways to put several models on 1 problem: Ultra: One lead delegates to supporting agents. Those agents report only to the lead. Multiagent: The same lead model as Ultra coordinates agents. They talk to each other and edit shared deliverables. Model Council: Several models answer the same question independently. Computer then shows where they agree and disagree. Model Council came to Computer in July 2026. Perplexity positions Multiagent for large, interconnected work that can run in parallel. Its examples include deal data room diligence, multi-scenario forecasts, annual report review, competing-hypothesis research and year-end tax preparation. How does it compare with other multi-agent products? Feature Perplexity Computer Multiagent Kimi Agent Swarm Manus Wide Research SuperGrok Heavy Max parallel agents 16 (plus lead) Up to 300 sub-agents “Hundreds”; tested up to 250 items Not disclosed Agent-to-agent communication Yes, direct, plus shared files Not disclosed Not disclosed (main agent assembles results) Agents compare work (per xAI launch claims) Models used Mixed vendors: Claude Opus 5.5, GPT 6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Carbon (default) Kimi K3 (K3 Swarm) Not disclosed Grok 4 Heavy Published performance data None 4.5x faster than single-agent sequential (K2.6) None Not disclosed for current version Platforms Web only Web and mobile app Web Not disclosed Plan / price Perplexity Max, $167/month billed annually Not disclosed Not disclosed $300/month at launch The clearest difference is model diversity. Perplexity mixes Anthropic, OpenAI and Google models in 1 team. Kimi and Grok run their own model families. Kimi trades depth of debate for scale, with up to 300 sub-agents. Deployment and availability Multiagent is available to all Perplexity Max subscribers. It runs on the web only. Users select Multiagent in Computer’s effort slider when starting a new task. Perplexity’s pricing page lists Max at $167 per month billed annually. Max includes 10,000 Computer credits per month. The launch post does not state credit cost per Multiagent task. Key Takeaways Multiagent is a new Computer effort level above Ultra. A lead runs up to 16 agents that share findings directly. Default team: Claude Opus 5.5, GPT 6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Carbon. GitLab enables organizations to increase developer productivity, improve operational efficiency, reduce security and compliance risk, and accelerate digital transformation. More than 50 million registered users and more than 50% of the Fortune 100* trust GitLab to ship better, more secure software faster.</p> <p>The same principles built into our products are reflected in how our team works: we embrace AI as a core productivity multiplier, with all team members expected to incorporate AI into their daily workflows to drive efficiency, innovation, and impact. GitLab is where careers accelerate, innovation flourishes, and every voice is valued. Our high-performance culture is driven by our values&nbsp;and continuous knowledge exchange, enabling our team members to reach their full potential while collaborating with industry leaders to solve complex problems. <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OuZIb5zszQI">Co-create the future with us</a> as we build technology that transforms how the world develops software.</p> <p>*<em>Fortune 500® is a registered trademark of Fortune Media IP Limited, used under license. Claim based on GitLab data. Fortune 100 refers to the top 20% ranked companies in the 2025 Fortune 500 list, published in June 2025. Fortune and Fortune Media IP Limited are not affiliated with, and do not endorse products or services of GitLab.</em></p></div><h4><strong>An overview of the role</strong></h4> <p>As Manager, Corporate Security - Platform Engineering, you'll lead a small, distributed team of security engineers and own programs that span Corporate Security teams. You'll define clear team boundaries, run security tooling through GitOps-based engineering practices, and bring program priorities, budgets, and vendor decisions to Security leadership. This is a hands-on technical leadership role: you won't be the primary implementer, but you'll write code, review designs and merge requests, make architecture decisions, and support incident response. This role is remote within North America, reports to the VP, Corporate Security, and is at job level M3 (Manager, Security Engineering).</p> <h4><strong>What you’ll do</strong></h4> <ul> <li>Lead, hire, coach, and develop security engineers, including Staff engineers setting technical direction in artificial intelligence (AI) security and cloud environments. Build clear career paths and support ownership, written communication, and psychological safety.</li> <li>Own the lifecycle of shared security tools, from evaluation and procurement through renewal and retirement. Use infrastructure-as-code repositories and GitOps practices, and give each tool a named owner, budget line, and exit plan. Initial priorities include Axonius, Push Security, Island, Material Security, the transition from Koi to Fleet osquery, and the CrowdStrike contract split with Security Operations.</li> <li>Lead the secure access service edge (SASE) and always-on virtual private network (VPN) rollout, and own data loss prevention policy. Coordinate Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) boundary decisions with Security Compliance, working with Endpoint Engineering on clients and device posture signals and Identity Engineering on Okta network-zone policy.</li> <li>Run the corporate email gateway and own domain-based message authentication, reporting, and conformance (DMARC), sender policy framework (SPF), and DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) across GitLab domains, including the FedRAMP tenant. Complete the separation of product email flow from corporate Google Workspace.</li> <li>Operate Sandbox Cloud across Amazon Web Services (AWS), Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP), including the self-service portal, demo and training environments, the SSP GitLab instance, and other gitlab.systems environments. Build automated deprovisioning and cost guardrails while keeping identity and access management with Identity Engineering and production infrastructure with Infrastructure Security and Site Reliability Engineering.</li> <li>Own Corporate Security's operating-model reporting, annual operating plan, software spend, change management, systems directory, handbook upkeep, and dashboards. Coordinate audit evidence across all three teams for Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX), System and Organization Controls 2 (SOC 2), and FedRAMP, replacing screenshots with code and query exports.</li> <li>Run departmental intake and reduce repeated requests through Slack automation, Serval, self-service security reviews, documentation hubs, and AI-assisted answers. Help each team focus on the systems it owns rather than routine triage.</li> <li>Represent Platform Engineering in Corporate Security and Security leadership forums, the Authorization to Operate Council, and monthly AI spend reviews. Partner with Corporate IT, Infrastructure Security, security incident response, Security Compliance, Security Risk, Enterprise AI, Legal and Privacy, Procurement, and Finance to resolve shared priorities and ownership questions.</li> </ul> <h4><strong>What you’ll bring</strong></h4> <ul> <li>Experience managing security or platform engineering teams across time zones, including hiring engineers and developing senior individual contributors. Experience defining a team's remit and redirecting work to the right owner.</li> <li>Experience owning several categories of corporate security tooling, such as network security, email security, software-as-a-service security posture, asset visibility, and cloud sandboxes. Sound judgment about when to adopt, consolidate, or retire tools.</li> <li>Experience leading a team that operates tools as code using Terraform or OpenTofu, GitOps, merge-request change management, continuous integration pipelines, and Python or a similar language. The technical depth to review designs and code.</li> <li>Hands-on experience deploying SASE, zero-trust network access, or always-on VPN solutions, alongside data loss prevention controls, in a remote-first company.</li> <li>Knowledge of AWS and GCP organization structures, account provisioning, guardrails, and cost controls sufficient to operate a self-service sandbox platform safely.</li> <li>Experience owning objectives and key results, vendor relationships, budgets, and security audit evidence programs, with the ability to write clear, concise plans for senior Security leadership.</li> <li>Experience using agentic AI tools in your work and a clear approach to governing AI tools, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and credentials. The ability to run an enablement program without becoming the approver for every tool.</li> <li>Clear written and asynchronous communication, a record of resolving ownership questions across functions, and an approach aligned with GitLab's values and all-remote, handbook-first ways of working. We welcome diverse backgrounds and transferable experience relevant to this work.</li> </ul> <h4><strong>About the team</strong></h4> <p>Platform Engineering owns shared

We are on an important mission to deliver the world’s best AI-native marketing solutions to our clients for remarkable business growth (without AI slop). The AI revolution has changed what’s possible and our proprietary system, built around 100+ API’s, makes it work. We are now looking for an <strong>expert engineer with exceptional creative taste</strong> to lead this system.</p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <h3><strong>Responsibilities</strong></h3> <ul> <li> <p>Lead the codebase and creative output of Elvoro’s proprietary social media engine</p> </li> <li> <p>Turn client briefs into large-scale short-form videos, carousels, static posts and ads</p> </li> <li> <p>Use your exceptional creative taste, knowledge on what type of content goes viral and converts well on social media, and large amounts of performance data to continuously, independently refine and improve the codebase to produce better content output.</p> </li> <li> <p>Schedule-post our high-quality content across numerous accounts using social media APIs</p> </li> <li> <p>Capture performance data via official APIs and use your creative taste and content conversion knowledge to refine content quality and test new creatives</p> </li> <li> <p>Maintain and extend the production codebase. Integrate numerous media and publishing APIs, test changes and monitor failures and cost per approved post</p> </li> <li> <p>Fix weak creative hooks, ai slop and pacing and product inaccuracies. Turn successful results into reusable yet unique systems</p> </li> <li> <p>Refine, manage and improve our code pipelines that produce thousands of different social media posts using unique processes</p> </li> </ul> <p>&nbsp;</p> <h3><strong>Tech Stack Qualifications</strong></h3> <p>Professional software engineering experience building and maintaining large production codebases.</p> <ul> <li> <p>Advanced <strong>Python</strong></p> </li> <li> <p>REST API integrations OAuth 2.0 (eg: Anthropic, Runway, SpaceXSI, Instagram, ...)</p> </li> <li> <p>Video, audio and image processing (FFmpeg, MoviePy, Pillow, ...)</p> </li> <li> <p>Google Cloud Storage (GCS)</p> </li> <li> <p>Git, GitHub, GitHub Actions</p> </li> <li> <p>Preferred: SQL, HTML/CSS, JavaScript (React)</p> </li> </ul> <p>&nbsp;</p> <h3><strong>AI-Native Workflow Qualifications</strong></h3> <ul> <li> <p>Strong prompt engineering skills. Proactively using AI for efficiency, speed, and quality. Agents such as: Claude Code, Cursor/xAI, Codex, etc.</p> </li> <li> <p>Judgment to manually review AI output and full accountability for all AI-generated code.</p> </li> </ul> <p>&nbsp;</p> <h3><strong>Benefits</strong></h3> <p>You get to lead Elvoro’s proprietary AI marketing engine and shape its technical and creative direction alongside the founder. An engineer previously working with Elvoro's founder has now gained a high-level job at Meta. Build a track record leading both engineering and creative production. You’ll lead campaigns for many established consumer brands and learn firsthand which creative decisions build brand awareness with hundreds of millions of views across social media and what turns attention into conversions such as sales and signups. oldContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Mon, 16 Nov 2026 18:00:13 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.12 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 Genesis AI Raises $500M At $3.5B Valuation To Bring Its Robots To Factories And Warehouses https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/robot-factory-workers-genesis-ai-fundraise/ Tue, 17 Nov 2026 14:00:18 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94396 Genesis AI , a startup teaching robots to perform physical tasks by learning from human movements, announced Tuesday it has raised $500 million in Series A funding at a $3.5 billion valuation. Premji Invest , Khosla Ventures and Eclipse co-led the round, which brings the company’s disclosed funding to $605 million since its 2024 inception. Genesis previously raised $105 million in a round announced in July 2025. The company is developing both robots and the AI software that controls them. Its approach combines recordings of human hand movements with training in simulated environments, where robots can practice skills before attempting them in the physical world. Genesis is initially targeting manufacturing, logistics and laboratories with its robot, Eno. Zhou Xian and Theophile Gervet, co-founders of Genesis AI. (Courtesy photo) “We just want to bring something more elegant, more timeless,” co-founder and CEO Zhou Xian told Crunchbase News in an interview. “In the end, this is a very full-stack company. … We have to build all different pieces across the entire stack to make sure we can tightly integrate our technology stack together, and hopefully build the most well-polished and reliable product. Other participants in the new financing include T. Rowe Price Associates , Durable Capital Partners , Bpifrance , HSG , Nvidia , AMD Ventures , Zoom , Samsung Next and Ericsson . Individual backers include Eric Schmidt , Eric Yuan , Jerry Yang , Xavier Niel and Zach Kirkhorn . The company plans to use the capital to expand its computing infrastructure, increase robot production and hire more employees, Xian told Crunchbase News. Presently, Genesis has close to 100 employees. It is headquartered in Paris, with offices in San Carlos, California. Venture funding to robotics startups has soared in 2026, with most of the investment going to companies based in China and the U.S., Crunchbase data shows. All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data. The closely related field of physical AI has also seen a surge in venture investment this year. Learning from human movements Genesis’s approach grew out of a challenge Xian encountered during his robotics research: The difficulty of finding enough examples for robots to learn from. Language models have vast amounts of text to draw on. But robots need a different kind of data to learn how to move and for example, pick up and handle objects. They also need that data to better understand what they’re touching and what happens when they act. Genesis works by using cameras and gloves to capture people’s hand and finger movements as they work, along with touch information. The company says its robotic hand closely matches the human hand and recording glove, making it easier for robots to learn those movements. Historically, collecting this kind of training data involves hiring people to remotely control robots, Xian said. Genesis aims to collect it from people doing their regular jobs instead. Those recordings help train the company’s AI model, GENE. Genesis also uses its simulation software, Genesis World, to train and test robot skills in virtual environments. The company claims this speeds up a process that would take longer with physical machines alone. From research project to robotics startup Genesis traces its origins to a research collaboration Xian started in 2022, also named Genesis, while he was pursuing a robotics Ph.D. at Carnegie Mellon University . The project brought together researchers from more than a dozen universities to develop robotics simulation tools. After graduating at the end of 2024, Xian teamed up with Theophile Gervet and decided to start a company. Genesis formally launched in March 2025 and expanded beyond simulation into AI software and robot hardware. Xian said developing those components together would help Genesis make them work reliably as a finished product. “That requires the intelligence, hardware and everything that goes into training and testing the robots to work as one system,” he said. Renting robots to businesses Genesis is exploring a rental model in which customers would pay for the robot and its software as a combined service. It has announced a partnership with LG CNS and has other Fortune 500 companies in its prospective customer pipeline, according to Xian. He declined to disclose revenue and did not provide a paying customer count. Premji Invest partner Vedant Agrawal said in a release that the firm was drawn to demonstrations of robots completing extended tasks independently. “Completing full tasks in real time, not just short clips, is what turns a robot into something a business can rely on,” he said. Genesis says it is ramping up Eno production for industrial customers. Looking ahead, it plans to expand into hospitality and healthcare, then consumer and outdoor uses. Now The Founder Is The Risk. https://news.crunchbase.com/startups/founder-venture-funding-pressure-meerbott-you-loud-clear/ Tue, 17 Nov 2026 12:00:45 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94394 By Kelly Meerbott The round closes. The announcement goes out. For about a week, everyone is happy. Then the pressure doubles. The number that used to be a hope is now a promise. The board that used to be patient now has a timeline. And the founder who just finished the hardest sales job of their life is expected to make the best decisions of their life, immediately, on less sleep than they’ve had in months. I’ve spent 17 years coaching about 1,500 leaders, including venture-backed founders. The pattern repeats often enough that I treat the first 90 days after a raise as a danger window. Founders don’t get complacent in that window. They get flooded, and most of them won’t say so out loud. What pressure does to judgment Kelly Meerbott of YOU – Loud & Clear. Neuroscientist Amy Arnsten’s review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience puts it plainly: “even quite mild acute uncontrollable stress can cause a rapid and dramatic loss of prefrontal cognitive abilities.” The prefrontal cortex weighs options and holds a plan steady. Notice the word uncontrollable. After a raise, a founder controls less than the cap table suggests: the hiring market, customer timelines, the board’s expectations. The founder hasn’t become less intelligent. The judgment that built the company is just harder to reach. Porcelli and Delgado , writing in Psychological Science, stressed volunteers with a hand in ice water then offered them financial gambles. They grew more cautious about potential gains and more willing to gamble on potential losses. It was a lab study, but I see the same shape in a founder six weeks after a Series B: hesitant about the bets that justified the round, and suddenly willing to roll the dice on anything

It also reopened a question investors have been circling for a while: Is ARR still the right way to describe an AI business? The limitations have been understood for some time. ARR was built for software companies selling predictable annual contracts, which is only part of how most AI companies make money. Through the early part of the generative AI boom, growth was steep enough that few people pressed the point. The OpenAI episode has made it harder to leave alone, partly because it showed how much weight public markets now place on a single private company’s numbers. For founders, this is worth paying attention to now rather than later. A cohort of AI companies is reaching the growth-capital stage, and the questions they face in diligence are changing. What ARR was built for Kenza Zayani of RTP Global. ARR became standard in the mid- to late-2000s, when software moved from licence fees to recurring subscriptions. A customer signed for 12 months, revenue became predictable and annualizing it was arithmetic rather than forecasting. The first generation of post-ChatGPT companies inherited it without much examination, despite earning money in a different way. Most now run hybrid models: a subscription base with consumption charges on top, billed against API calls, tokens processed or compute used. A growing number charge per outcome. An annualized figure blends revenue a customer has committed to with revenue that depends on what they use next month. What gets presented as ARR is usually a revenue run rate: recent revenue multiplied out to an annual figure. That is a reasonable way to describe momentum, and a less reliable guide to the year ahead. The first question an investor tends to ask is what the figure actually counts. Companies that sell partly through partners can report either the full value of those sales or only the share they keep, and the two conventions produce very different numbers for the same business. Both are legitimate, but the two are not necessarily comparable. Take two companies both reporting a $10 million annualized run rate. In the first, most of that revenue is contracted, and comes from customers whose usage has expanded steadily over 12 months. In the second, it rests on a handful of customers whose consumption spiked in the last quarter. These are not similar businesses. The first has demonstrated that customers keep coming back and spending more. Nothing in the headline figure tells you that. Looking beyond the headline If a single figure cannot separate those two businesses, the question is what can. The answer depends on the stage. At pre-seed and seed, the number matters. A steep trajectory can point to market demand, to customers willing to pay, and to a team beginning to crack go-to-market. A run rate isn’t generally expected to predict the year at that size. Later you need more. What matters is the revenue behind the number: customer concentration, how much is contracted rather than consumed, how predictable that revenue is, and whether the gross margins hold as volume rises. Retention and expansion are the centerpiece. They tell you how essential a product has become and whether it will still be in use in a few years. Churn is diagnostic in a way a growth figure never is. It can point to demand the product is not answering, pricing that does not match the value, a need that was never really recurring, or a market shallower than it first looked. What investors will expect next ARR has been a staple of how high-growth tech companies demonstrate momentum for such a long time that it’s not likely to disappear anytime soon. What is changing is how much weight that single number can carry on its own. Expect more investors to ask what a figure actually counts, how much of it is committed revenue, and what retention looks like by cohort. The founders who have those answers ready will tell a much more convincing story than a single number ever could. Kenza Zayani is an early-stage investor at RTP Global , based in London. She is drawn to ambitious founders tackling the most challenging problems, with a particular interest in AI from infrastructure to applications. Zayani has built experience in venture capital across stages, and at RTP Global, she brings her multistage experience and data-driven approach to company building with founders. The post Perplexity Computer Adds Multiagent: Up to 16 AI Agents That Cross-Check Work appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Perplexity has added Multiagent to Computer , its agent platform for research and multistep work. Perplexity Computer Multiagent is a new effort level that sits above Ultra. A lead agent runs a team of agents on different frontier models. Those agents work in parallel, share findings directly and check each other’s work. For developers and analysts, the change is structural. Supporting agents no longer report only to a single lead. TL;DR Size: Up to 16 agents per task, plus the lead. Context length: Not disclosed. Runs on: Perplexity’s cloud. Web only, Perplexity Max plan. No local or quantized option. Performance: Not benchmarked. Perplexity published no accuracy or speed numbers. Best: 16-agent cap with direct agent-to-agent checks across 3 default model families (Claude, GPT, Gemini). What is Perplexity Computer Multiagent? Multiagent is the highest effort level in Perplexity Computer. It coordinates AI models to analyze complex tasks and cross-check their work, per Perplexity’s announcement . It builds on effort controls launched on September 17, 2026 . That release added 4 settings: Light, Standard, High and Ultra. Each setting picks the orchestrator model and its reasoning depth. Lower settings use less expensive models. How does Multiagent work? The lead agent plans the task and assigns parts to supporting agents. It can assign up to 16 agents and also does part of the work itself. In Perplexity’s example, Claude Fable 5.2 plans the task. It splits work among agents running Claude Opus 5.5, GPT 6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Carbon. Those 3 models form the default team. Fable 5.2 and GPT 6 Astra join as supporting agents only when requested or needed. Key mechanics from the launch post : Direct sharing: Agents use evidence found by others, question assumptions and flag discrepancies. Shared files: Agents coordinate edits to shared files. One agent can update revenue assumptions and notify another to reuse them in a valuation. Single point of contact: Users talk only to the lead. The lead merges findings into one response. Follow-ups: The lead tells affected agents what changed. The team continues its existing work. Control: Users see which agents and models are running. Stopping the thread stops the whole team. Model choice: Users can name specific models in their query. Multiagent vs Ultra vs Model Council Perplexity now offers 3 ways to put several models on 1 problem: Ultra: One lead delegates to supporting agents. Those agents report only to the lead. Multiagent: The same lead model as Ultra coordinates agents. They talk to each other and edit shared deliverables. Model Council: Several models answer the same question independently. Computer then shows where they agree and disagree. Model Council came to Computer in July 2026. Perplexity positions Multiagent for large, interconnected work that can run in parallel. Its examples include deal data room diligence, multi-scenario forecasts, annual report review, competing-hypothesis research and year-end tax preparation. How does it compare with other multi-agent products? Feature Perplexity Computer Multiagent Kimi Agent Swarm Manus Wide Research SuperGrok Heavy Max parallel agents 16 (plus lead) Up to 300 sub-agents “Hundreds”; tested up to 250 items Not disclosed Agent-to-agent communication Yes, direct, plus shared files Not disclosed Not disclosed (main agent assembles results) Agents compare work (per xAI launch claims) Models used Mixed vendors: Claude Opus 5.5, GPT 6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Carbon (default) Kimi K3 (K3 Swarm) Not disclosed Grok 4 Heavy Published performance data None 4.5x faster than single-agent sequential (K2.6) None Not disclosed for current version Platforms Web only Web and mobile app Web Not disclosed Plan / price Perplexity Max, $167/month billed annually Not disclosed Not disclosed $300/month at launch The clearest difference is model diversity. Perplexity mixes Anthropic, OpenAI and Google models in 1 team. Kimi and Grok run their own model families. Kimi trades depth of debate for scale, with up to 300 sub-agents. Deployment and availability Multiagent is available to all Perplexity Max subscribers. It runs on the web only. Users select Multiagent in Computer’s effort slider when starting a new task. Perplexity’s pricing page lists Max at $167 per month billed annually. Max includes 10,000 Computer credits per month. The launch post does not state credit cost per Multiagent task. Key Takeaways Multiagent is a new Computer effort level above Ultra. A lead runs up to 16 agents that share findings directly. Default team: Claude Opus 5.5, GPT 6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Carbon. Max-only, web-only, with no published benchmarks. Best fit: data room diligence and multi-scenario forecasting. Check out the official announcement , the effort controls post and Perplexity pricing . The GPT-6.2 Astra model is the new frontier tier for hard, long-horizon tasks. GPT-6.2 Sol is the efficient everyday tier. For developers, the key point is cost per task. The post New LoRA Adapter Lifts Qwen3.8 Coding Success From 39% to 65% appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Hugging Face’s harness-hub team has released Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted , a LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B . It was trained with reinforcement learning to work inside the pi coding agent . The Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted LoRA adapter targets one harness instead of general chat. For developers running local coding agents, that is the point. You keep the open base model and swap in a small, harness-specific adapter. TL;DR Size: LoRA rank 32 (alpha 64) on Qwen3.8-27B, a 27B dense hybrid with 262,144 native context. Merged BF16 checkpoint is about 54 GB. Runs on: vLLM with LoRA enabled, or llama.cpp with a GGUF adapter on a Q8_0 base. Inference VRAM is not disclosed. Training used 2x NVIDIA B200. Performance: Large pass@1 gains inside pi with thinking off, plus far shorter sessions. Best: 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), up from 39.2%. Worst: 55.8% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The base model with thinking already reaches 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro. Bottom line: Best: thinking-level accuracy at about 4.5x fewer tokens. Worst: small eval sets, self-reported, pi only. What is Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted? Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted is a PEFT LoRA adapter that turns Qwen3.8-27B into a model tuned for pi. pi is an MIT-licensed agent toolkit with a coding agent CLI. The adapter is released under Apache-2.0 . It applies to the q, k, v, o, gate, up and down projections. It only works on Qwen3.8-27B. The base model is a dense hybrid . It alternates Gated DeltaNet linear-attention blocks with Gated Attention blocks across 64 layers. How does the harness adapter training work? The method comes from Hugging Face’s harness adapters post from November 6. The idea is 1 LoRA adapter per model and harness. Training runs inside the unmodified harness on verifiable tasks. For this checkpoint, the model card lists these details: Algorithm: AsyncGRPO from TRL , 8 rollouts per task at temperature 0.8. Tasks: 750 scale800 tasks interleaved with 300 TermGrade tasks. Reward: verifier correctness plus a tool-efficiency bonus with weight 0.1. Budget: up to 50 agent steps and 1,800 seconds per rollout, thinking off. Checkpoint: step 160. The run stopped at step 191 of 1,000 planned. Every tool call passes through safeagents , a rule-based proxy. It blocks calls such as fetching benchmark answers from the Hub. Blocked rollouts score 0, so RL pushes the model away from reward hacking. Benchmarks: how much does the LoRA adapter help? All numbers below are self-reported. They use the pi harness, 1 attempt per task. Benchmark (pi, thinking off) Base Qwen3.8-27B pi-adapted Change SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 39.2% 64.7% +25.5 ± 14.2 pts (p = 0.0023) Terminal-Bench 2.1 (86 tasks) 39.5% 55.8% +16.3 ± 9.1 pts (p = 0.0013) The adapter solved 15 new SWE-bench Pro tasks and lost 2. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, it gained 16 and lost 2. Efficiency is the larger story. On tasks both models solved, median turns fell from 59 to 23 on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, they fell from 18 to 8. The adapter also generates about 4.5x fewer tokens than the base model with thinking. How does it compare with thinking mode and other adapters? With thinking on, the base model already scores 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro and 54.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. So the adapter matches thinking-level accuracy without paying for long reasoning traces. With thinking on, the adapter reaches 66.7% and 56.6%. How do you deploy it? The model card gives 4 routes: vLLM: serve Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B with --enable-lora --max-lora-rank 32 , thinking disabled. Point pi at http://localhost:8000/v1 . llama.cpp: load the GGUF adapter on a Q8_0 base GGUF. Llama.app on macOS: register the adapter with a 32,768-token context. Merge: merge with PEFT on CPU, then serve the 54 GB BF16 result without LoRA flags. Because adapters share 1 base model, a single server can host pi and OpenCode adapters side by side. Key Takeaways Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted is an Apache-2.0, rank-32 RL LoRA for the pi agent. SWE-bench Pro hard-51 rises from 39.2% to 64.7%, thinking off. Median turns drop from 59 to 23 on SWE-bench Pro. It matches base-with-thinking accuracy at about 4.5x fewer tokens. Results are self-reported on small sets; the tweet’s 29.4% baseline was corrected. It also reopened a question investors have been circling for a while: Is ARR still the right way to describe an AI business? The limitations have been understood for some time. ARR was built for software companies selling predictable annual contracts, which is only part of how most AI companies make money. Through the early part of the generative AI boom, growth was steep enough that few people pressed the point. The OpenAI episode has made it harder to leave alone, partly because it showed how much weight public markets now place on a single private company’s numbers. For founders, this is worth paying attention to now rather than later. A cohort of AI companies is reaching the growth-capital stage, and the questions they face in diligence are changing. What ARR was built for Kenza Zayani of RTP Global. ARR became standard in the mid- to late-2000s, when software moved from licence fees to recurring subscriptions. A customer signed for 12 months, revenue became predictable and annualizing it was arithmetic rather than forecasting. The first generation of post-ChatGPT companies inherited it without much examination, despite earning money in a different way. Most now run hybrid models: a subscription base with consumption charges on top, billed against API calls, tokens processed or compute used. A growing number charge per outcome. An annualized figure blends revenue a customer has committed to with revenue that depends on what they use next month. What gets presented as ARR is usually a revenue run rate: recent revenue multiplied out to an annual figure. That is a reasonable way to describe momentum, and a less reliable guide to the year ahead. The first question an investor tends to ask is what the figure actually counts. Companies that sell partly through partners can report either the full value of those sales or only the share they keep, and the two conventions produce very different numbers for the same business. Both are legitimate, but the two are not necessarily comparable. Take two companies both reporting a $10 million annualized run rate. In the first, most of that revenue is contracted, and comes from customers whose usage has expanded steadily over 12 months. In the second, it rests on a handful of customers whose consumption spiked in the last quarter. These are not similar businesses. The first has demonstrated that customers keep coming back and spending more. Nothing in the headline figure tells you that. Looking beyond the headline If a single figure cannot separate those two businesses, the question is what can. The answer depends on the stage. At pre-seed and seed, the number matters. A steep trajectory can point to market demand, to customers willing to pay, and to a team beginning to crack go-to-market. A run rate isn’t generally expected to predict the year at that size. Later you need more. What matters is the revenue behind the number: customer concentration, how much is contracted rather than consumed, how predictable that revenue is, and whether the gross margins hold as volume rises. Retention and expansion are the centerpiece. They tell you how essential a product has become and whether it will still be in use in a few years. Churn is diagnostic in a way a growth figure never is. It can point to demand the product is not answering, pricing that does not match the value, a need that was never really recurring, or a market shallower than it first looked. What investors will expect next ARR has been a staple of how high-growth tech companies demonstrate momentum for such a long time that it’s not likely to disappear anytime soon. What is changing is how much weight that single number can carry on its own. Expect more investors to ask what a figure actually counts, how much of it is committed revenue, and what retention looks like by cohort. The founders who have those answers ready will tell a much more convincing story than a single number ever could. Kenza Zayani is an early-stage investor at RTP Global , based in London. She is drawn to ambitious founders tackling the most challenging problems, with a particular interest in AI from infrastructure to applications. Zayani has built experience in venture capital across stages, and at RTP Global, she brings her multistage experience and data-driven approach to company building with founders. newContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Wed, 18 Nov 2026 19:39:58 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.12 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 The Key Numbers I’m Watching As Anthropic Makes Its IPO Debut https://news.crunchbase.com/ai/anthropic-ant-ipo-revenue-growth-risks-s1-analysis/ Wed, 18 Nov 2026 19:39:58 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94421 Anthropic starts trading on the Nasdaq tomorrow with a growth story that’s unlike any I’ve seen in close to three decades working in Silicon Valley: The company says revenue reached $17 billion in Q3, less than four years after Claude launched with zero. The San Francisco-based company also presents a stark contrast to the more common theme in recent years of venture-backed companies staying private longer: Anthropic is less than six years old as it goes public in a potentially record-setting listing. Those metrics are impressive, but there are other numbers in its S-1 I keep circling, too, like the nearly $900 billion in compute purchase and lease commitments. I’ve worked in Silicon Valley through the dot-com boom and bust, the rise of SaaS, social media, unicorn and decacorn startups and now, AI. Anthropic’s extraordinary rise and entrance onto the public markets marks a new technology era — one with enormous growth and potential, but also tremendous costs, risks and unknowns. OpenAI ’s seminal success was the launch of chatbots in 2022 — within two months, ChatGPT reached 100 million users and in less than four years, OpenAI had a billion monthly active users. By contrast, Anthropic’s breakout was the success of Claude Code, launched just last year. Already, Anthropic says 11,900 companies use the product, spending $100,000 or more trailing 12 months, up 12x from a year ago. In its S-1 , the company says that marks the fastest enterprise adoption for any company on record. Anthropic’s IPO could value it at $1.4 trillion and raise $88.5 billion via the IPO and concurrent private placement. As it becomes public, I’ll be watching closely to see if the company can keep turning demand for Claude and Claude Code into a durable business while building out the astounding amount of compute it says it needs and managing the many risks that surround its technology. By the numbers Here are some of the other key details and figures that caught my eye ahead of Anthropic’s first day on the public markets: The company has a purchase and lease agreement for $895.4 billion for compute. Of that, $447.5 billion will be incurred before the end of 2030. Anthropic currently has over $100 billion on its balance sheet. Its IPO seeks to add another roughly $100 billion, creating a war chest for those compute commitments. When it launched Claude in the first quarter of 2023, Anthropic had zero revenue. In less than four years, revenue reached $17 billion in Q3 2026, up 12x from Q3 2025. More than 1,900 customers spend more than $1 million and 250 more than $10 million, trailing 12 months, according to the company. Its per-employee revenue figures are impressive: Each employee supports $6.6 million in trailing 12-month revenue as of Sept 30, 2026. Anthropic is putting aside 5% of equity for a fund devoted to public good, adding 2% for every 50% increase in share price. Each founder is selling roughly $250 million worth of shares in the listing, depending on its final listing price. The backers behind Anthropic’s rise Anthropic got to where it is now through a fast sequence of funding rounds, from its Jaan Tallinn -led Series A in 2021 to its Series H in May of this year that valued the company at $965 billion. Other lead investors over its many funding rounds include Google , Amazon , Spark Capital , Menlo Ventures , Lightspeed Venture Partners , Coatue and Sequoia Capital, all of whom are slated to be among the winners when it goes public tomorrow. Risks, opportunities and what’s ahead The AI era has the potential to generate massive amounts of new wealth and unlock life-changing technological advances. But it also comes with huge risks. Anthropic’s S-1 captures that tension. The opportunity the company describes extends far beyond coding and software. It says its focus in 2027 will be AI agents for knowledge work and scientific discovery. It also points to potential gains in biology and rare-disease research, economic growth, wider access to health care and improved government services. The S-1 cites the World Health Organization ’s estimate that 4.6 billion people lack access to basic health services. That promise comes with a competitive risk for its customers, too: Companies may worry that data they share with AI providers could help train models that compete with their products, or that more capable models could erode parts of their existing businesses. Anthropic’s S-1 also flags risks ranging from cyber and biological attacks to unpredictable model behavior, authoritarian surveillance and economic disruption. Anthropic’s public-benefit structure is meant to balance those competing pressures. As a public benefit corporation, the company says it must weigh commercial success against the public good. Its founders, employees and Long-Term Benefit Trust share in governance; the trust has no financial stake and weighs impacts on national security, economics, global health and science. Anthropic points to its launch of Mythos as an example of that balance. As Anthropic debuts tomorrow, I’ll be watching how well it balances AI’s promise with the risks its own filing lays out.
